A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same xFinder/KAF research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable matching despite the changed title, formatting, and appendix organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original extraction experiments with 19 fine-tuned models and downstream evaluations of 10 LLMs, including detailed results in Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds judgment-accuracy, execution-time, and cost results in Section 5.2.

M1.justification: The KAF-based QLoRA training, input fields, extracted-answer output, and two augmentation procedures remain unchanged. The xFinder prompt is retained from Appendix E.3 to F.4. Answer matching already appeared in v1's pipeline; the revised evaluator framing does not establish a new procedure.

E1.justification: The same source datasets, four answer formats, generalization scenarios, and downstream tasks are retained. The change from 18 to 19 datasets in Section 4.1 corrects the narrative: v1 Table 3 already lists the same 19 datasets as v3 Table 7. EVOUNA is newly discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds evaluated comparisons with PandaLM-7B, JudgeLM-7B/13B/33B, and GPT-4 as a judge with and without CoT. v1 evaluated the three RegEx frameworks and GPT-4 as an extractor; those extraction comparators remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces judgment accuracy against human annotations, reference-answer judging prompts, a GPT-4 CoT condition, and timing/cost measurements using 200 questions per answer type. Existing training and downstream settings are retained. The new Table 16 lists unrestricted test prompts, conflicting with retained footnote 5; this does not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds focused analyses of the judgment-versus-extraction accuracy gap, GPT-4 judging with CoT, and evaluation time and cost in Tables 3–6. These supplement the retained generalization, model-size, ranking, and answer-format analyses rather than introducing a broad new ablation or robustness program.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional timing averages summarize answer categories rather than repeated-run variability.

E6.justification: Original extraction scores, downstream result tables, and ranking plots are unchanged. New Table 3 reports judgment accuracy of 97.61% for xFinder-llama38it, 97.48% for xFinder-qwen1505, 51.90% for PandaLM-7B, and 88.42% for GPT-4 with CoT. Tables 4–6 add accuracy gaps and timing/cost results. These are new measurements, not improvements in the retained extraction scores.

T1.justification: Section 3's definitions and Equations 1–6 are retained. Appendix D.1 adds a logical assertion that error-free matching makes correct extraction necessary and sufficient for correct judgment, together with reasoning about the accuracy gap. The necessity assertion conflicts with its own example of incorrect extraction producing a correct judgment.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the principal contribution from robust extraction relative to RegEx frameworks to an evaluator claimed to outperform judge models in judgment accuracy and evaluation efficiency. The original KAF, extraction-accuracy, and evaluation-reliability claims are retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds the substantive interpretation that correct judgments can conceal extraction errors and uses the accuracy gap as a reliability diagnostic. It also interprets cost results as supporting greater efficiency and flexibility. Meanwhile, v1 Section 6's explicit warning about deployment costs even for the 500M model, and its compression/CPU-deployment discussion, disappear rather than move.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds detailed split composition by model, dataset, answer type, and prompt; annotation guidelines and disagreement handling; and sample records. Appendix F.3 supplies judging prompts, and Section 5.2 documents timing hardware and process allocation. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained dataset or training procedure.

R1.justification: Related work adds EVOUNA and supporting citations concerning internal consistency, TurtleBench, and attention heads. The existing discussion of fine-tuned judges and the claimed first systematic study of reliable evaluation largely remain, making this a limited expansion of the literature context.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, front-matter prose and terminology are revised, experimental setup is collected into a summary, and annotation material is reorganized into a dedicated KAF appendix. Much of the existing formal definition, method, downstream analysis, and prompt wording remains, so the revision to existing prose and narrative structure is limited.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are substantially redrawn, and the document adopts ICLR formatting with restyled tables and repositioned captions. New displays include judgment/gap/cost tables, twelve dataset-composition tables, an annotation-interface figure, and two judge-prompt figures. Existing ranking charts are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The new correctness and cost comparisons strengthen the empirical assessment, while detailed KAF composition and annotation instructions substantially improve auditability. These benefits are tempered by removal of the deployment-cost limitation, conflicting test-prompt descriptions in Table 16 and footnote 5, and Appendix D.1's flawed necessity claim about extraction and judgment. The resulting net improvement is useful but limited.
